summary: This document reserves the top-level domain label "alt" for use in non-DNS contexts. It also gives advice to developers building alternative naming systems. Names ending in .alt are not meant to be looked up in the global DNS.

eli5.summary: The internet phone book set aside one made-up neighborhood name, .alt, that real phone books won't ever list. People inventing their own naming games can use it safely.

questions: can i use .alt for my own naming system
subtitle: A reserved top-level label that says: this name is not in the global DNS, so do not look it up there.

tldr.problem: Many systems use DNS-looking names that are not part of the global DNS, and queries for those names leak to resolvers and root servers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9476 reserves the label alt as a special-use domain name and as an unmanaged pseudo-TLD, so names ending in .alt signal a non-DNS namespace that should not be resolved with DNS.
tldr.outcome: Projects with alternative namespaces get a designated place to put them. The RFC creates no registry and no governance for names under .alt, and warns that such names will still leak.

today: RFC 9476 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2023, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the definition of the .alt special-use name.

sections.title: Why Reserve .alt
sections.content:
Names that look like DNS names, a series of labels separated by dots, are now common even in systems that are not part of the global DNS administered by IANA. RFC 9476 reserves the top-level label alt (short for alternative) as a special-use domain name under RFC 6761. Used as the rightmost label, it signals that the name is not rooted in the global DNS and should not be resolved using the DNS protocol.

The techniques address some of the issues discussed in RFC 8244. The authors chose .alt rather than something like alt.arpa so that users do not have to worry that a parent of their name would be resolved if the name leaked to the Internet.
sections.eli5: Some people invent their own address books that look like web addresses. Ending a name with .alt says 'this one is not in the normal address book.'

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content: The RFC defines a few terms. A DNS context is the namespace anchored at the globally unique DNS root and administered by IANA. A non-DNS context is any other, alternative namespace. A pseudo-TLD is a label in the position of a TLD that is not part of the global DNS; the term is not meant to be pejorative.
sections.eli5: The normal internet address book is the DNS context. Any other address book is a non-DNS context, and .alt marks entries from those.

sections.title: The .alt Namespace
sections.content:
The .alt label is reserved as an unmanaged pseudo-TLD namespace. In DNS wire format it corresponds to a 0x03616c7400 suffix, while wire formats of non-DNS protocols might be different. DNS stub and recursive resolvers do not need to look these names up in the DNS context. The RFC suggests, but does not require, that non-DNS protocols follow DNS name syntax.

Groups creating a new alternative namespace may do so under a label of their own beneath .alt. The RFC defines neither a registry nor a governance model, since the space is not managed by the IETF or IANA. There is no guarantee of unambiguous mappings from names to resolution mechanisms, and handling collisions is outside the IETF's remit. Existing projects using pseudo-TLDs are recommended, but not required, to move under .alt.

The RFC says plainly that names under .alt will leak outside their context and reach recursive resolvers and root servers. Such queries always elicit NXDOMAIN, which wastes resources. Aggressive use of DNSSEC-validated caches (RFC 8198) and QNAME minimization (RFC 9156) can reduce that traffic.
sections.eli5: Anyone can make their own club under the .alt name, but nobody keeps a list or settles arguments if two clubs pick the same name. And some letters will still end up at the wrong post office.

sections.title: IANA Registration and Reservation Answers
sections.content:
IANA added .alt to the Special-Use Domain Name registry with a reference to this RFC. The RFC also answers the questions that RFC 6761 poses for such reservations, noting that they were written with DNS resolution in mind.

  • Software built for an alternative namespace under .alt is expected to have its own processing rules, probably in specialized resolver APIs or libraries. Other software is not expected to treat the names as special.
  • Caching and authoritative DNS servers SHOULD NOT recognize .alt names as special or give them special handling.
  • DNS server operators treat these names like any other TLD not in the global DNS, though they may notice that a query was leaked and use that for debugging.
  • Registries and registrars cannot register DNS names under .alt, because it will not exist in the global DNS root.
sections.eli5: The official list of reserved names now includes .alt. Ordinary phone-book servers should just treat it like any unknown name.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Names under .alt will undoubtedly leak into the global DNS, and the RFC calls this a general problem of alternative namespaces. A name such as example.alt could cause a privacy issue for names in that namespace that leak. If a name ending in .alt is sufficiently unique, long-lasting and frequently leaks, it can act like a web cookie, with the downsides of identification or re-identification.

Security is addressed briefly. Since .alt names are explicitly outside the DNS context, DNS-related security considerations cannot be relied on. Care must be taken when mapping the pseudo-TLD into its non-DNS resolution system to obtain whatever security that system offers.
sections.eli5: If you invent a very unusual secret name and it escapes to the open internet, people can recognize it and tell it is you, a bit like a nametag.
